why.Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan: When coming from the west side or linking the climb into a Ptarmigan Traverse trip, accepting a longer, rougher approach than the ferry and Agnes Creek line.

review.notes: Primary agrees with prior research; why written from stored notes only.
fromStoredNotes: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor

why.Chewuch River trail from Thirtymile: When you want a loop, walking in on this trail and out over Andrews Pass or the reverse; confirm the road to Thirtymile is open first.

review.notes: Andrews Creek is the better documented standard; Thirtymile is similar length but has had road access problems.

why.Chewuch River trail from Thirtymile: When you want a loop, walking in on this trail and out over Andrews Pass or the reverse; confirm the road to Thirtymile is open first.

review.notes: Same approaches as the North Ridge; Andrews Creek is the usual one.

why.Harts Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail s: To skip the brushy, slow lower West Fork Methow trail by starting high at Harts Pass and walking the crest trail south to Horse Heaven.
why.Canyon Creek and Mill Creek from SR-20: When you want to start straight from the highway and can put up with an overgrown Mill Creek trail and slow alder route-finding.

review.notes: Reports of overgrown trail on both the Mill Creek and Methow approaches; the marked primary is the shared upper section.

why.From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Can: Only for parties already in Canada who have confirmed a lawful border crossing; much shorter, but the tread is overgrown after the first mile or two.

review.notes: Hannegan Pass line is the US standard per stored notes and prior research; the Canadian line is never primary.
fromStoredNotes: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

why.Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass: When the upper Harts Pass road is not usable, or for a loop trip, starting from a much lower trailhead and joining the standard line in the Middle Fork valley.
why.Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap: For an eastern line off the Monument Creek trail into the open basin below the peak, putting up with slow going lower down instead of staging from Shellrock Basin.

review.notes: No useful search done; reasons taken from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap basin

why.Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valle: When you reach the area through Stehekin, by boat or over Cascade Pass, since it means far less walking than the Thunder Creek approach once you are in the valley.

fromStoredNotes: Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valley

why.Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments: To avoid the loose, snow-prone grind of Aasgard Pass, trading roughly two extra miles and a thousand feet of gain for a gentler, more gradual walk.

review.notes: Search agrees Snow Lakes is longer and more gradual; Aasgard is shorter but steeper. Many parties combine one way in with the other out.

why.Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Ba: When starting from the Alpental side or wanting a steeper snow line, early in the season while the gully still holds snow and an axe and crampons are needed.

review.notes: Source Lake gully approach confirmed in use; the rest is from stored notes.

why.Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valle: For a more direct way to the Napeequa side than the long High Pass traverse, best when the Chiwawa River is low enough to ford safely.

review.notes: Evidence is split on which is more used.

problems: A Mountaineers route page lists Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley as its Southwest Route approach (about 20 miles, 6,000 ft), so it may be at least as common as the marked Buck Creek Pass and High Pass primary, which is a much longer traverse. Owner to decide; primary left unchanged.

why.Burgundy Col in a single push: When doing the col and the climb in one long day without carrying overnight gear to the bench camp, at the price of a heavy pack on the loose scree.

review.notes: Both ways walk the same line; the primary is the camp variant.
fromStoredNotes: Burgundy Col in a single push

problems: The two ways follow the same path and differ only in whether you camp at the bench. The camp is marked primary, which matches the stored note calling it the usual way; no change proposed, but the two are really one approach.

why.Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Cre: When you want much less distance than the Snow Lakes walk and can handle a full day of brushy, trail-less navigation with cliff bands.

review.notes: Reason from stored notes; prior research agrees the Snow Lakes line is standard.
fromStoredNotes: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
